title: Zero & First Conditionals
subtitle: Talk about general truths, and about real possibilities in the future.
objectives: Form the zero conditional for general truths and facts
Form the first conditional for real, possible future situations
Tell the two apart based on meaning

content.intro: "If" sentences let you connect a condition to a result. These first two types are the most common in everyday English.

rules.heading: a) Zero conditional — general truths
rules.body:
If + present simple, present simple. Used for things that are always true (facts, habits, science).

  • If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
  • If it rains, the streets get wet.

rules.heading: b) First conditional — real future possibility
rules.body:
If + present simple, will + base verb. Used for something that could realistically happen in the future.

  • If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
  • If she studies hard, she will pass the exam.

examples: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If she studies hard, she always gets good grades.
If they finish their work on time, they will go to the party.
If you don't water plants, they die.
If I have time this weekend, I will call you.

commonMistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
commonMistakes.right: If it rains, we will stay home.
commonMistakes.why: The "if" clause never uses "will" — use the present simple, even though the meaning is future.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you heat water, it will boil at 100°C. (as a general fact)
commonMistakes.right: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
commonMistakes.why: A general, always-true fact needs the zero conditional (present + present), not "will."

commonMistakes.wrong: If she study hard, she will pass.
commonMistakes.right: If she studies hard, she will pass.
commonMistakes.why: Third person singular (she) still needs -s in the "if" clause.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct zero or first conditional form.

items.prompt: If you ___ (heat) water to 100 degrees, it ___ (boil).
items.explanation: A general scientific fact — zero conditional, present + present.

items.prompt: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we ___ (stay) at home.
items.explanation: A real future possibility — first conditional, present + will.

items.prompt: If she ___ (study) hard, she always ___ (get) good grades.
items.explanation: A general truth about her — zero conditional.

items.prompt: If they ___ (finish) their work on time, they ___ (go) to the party.
items.explanation: A real future possibility — first conditional.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a general, always-true fact?
options: If it rains tomorrow, I will bring an umbrella.
If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
If she calls, I will answer.
items.explanation: Mixing colors is a general fact — zero conditional.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes a real possibility for the future?
options: If water freezes, it becomes ice.
If I have time this weekend, I will call you.
If plants don't get water, they die.
items.explanation: This describes a specific, possible future event — first conditional.

items.incorrect: If it will rain, we will stay home.
answer: If it rains, we will stay home.
items.explanation: The "if" clause never uses "will," even when talking about the future.

items.incorrect: If she study hard, she will pass the exam.
answer: If she studies hard, she will pass the exam.
items.explanation: Third person singular needs -s in the "if" clause.

summary: Zero conditional: If + present, present — for general truths and facts.
First conditional: If + present, will + base verb — for real future possibilities.
The "if" clause never uses "will," in either type.
